name: Fruit and veg smell diet

lead: Some people eat more fruit and vegetables to make their natural scent more pleasant. A study of men found higher fruit and vegetable intake associated with sweat rated floral, fruity, sweet and medicinal in quality.
Dietary compounds appear in sweat and may change how it smells, though the specific mechanism is not detailed in the sources consulted. The scents are described as mild rather than strong.

paras: People simply increase fruit and vegetable servings in their regular meals, often as part of a broader healthy-eating or grooming routine. The change builds gradually as diet shifts.
No risks are documented in the sources consulted. The effect is described as mild, and diet changes that are large may need nutrition guidance for people with medical conditions.

web.title: The effect of meat consumption on body odor attractiveness (Europe PMC record)

angle.text: Users eat more fruit and vegetables so that diet-derived compounds in sweat give a more pleasant natural scent. A study of men associated higher intake with sweat rated floral, fruity and sweet, with the effect described as mild.

lead: The fruit and veg smell diet is the practice of eating more fruit and vegetables in the belief that it makes sweat and body odor smell more pleasant. The aim is to be more attractive up close, which is part of overall presentation. Wikipedia's body odor article reports a 2017 study by Zuniga, Stevenson, Mahmut and Stephen in Evolution and Human Behavior, titled Diet quality and the attractiveness of male body odor, in which men who ate more fruit and vegetables had sweat described as more pleasant, with floral, fruity, sweet and medicinal qualities [1].

Body odor arises mainly when skin bacteria such as Corynebacterium break down compounds secreted by apocrine sweat glands, and Wikipedia lists food, drink, gut microbiome and genetics among the factors that can alter it, along with hygiene [1]. Grokipedia likewise says fruit- and vegetable-rich diets have been associated with more pleasant body odors, though the scents are not typically strong [2].

A related line of research examined meat: a 2006 study in Chemical Senses had 17 men eat a red-meat and a non-meat diet for two weeks each, and women rated the odor from the non-meat diet as more attractive, more pleasant and less intense [3].
infobox: Zuniga et al., 2017, Evolution and Human Behavior [1]
Non-meat diet odor rated more attractive than red-meat diet odor (Havlicek and Lenochova, 2006) [3]

paras: Apocrine sweat itself is largely odorless; the typical smell comes from skin bacteria converting secreted compounds into volatile acids, including butyric, propionic and isovaleric acids [1]. Because diet changes what the body excretes and may influence the skin microbiome, researchers have asked whether foods change perceived odor [1].

The Zuniga study associated higher fruit and vegetable consumption with more pleasant sweat in men [1]. Sample details are not given in the reference pages consulted. The Havlicek and Lenochova experiment used a within-subject design with 17 male donors on a meat and a non-meat diet for two weeks each, with women not using hormonal contraceptives rating the samples [3]. The authors concluded that red meat consumption negatively affects perceived pleasantness of body odor [3].

No studies found of fruit and vegetable intake as an intervention for body odor beyond the observational and experimental work described above. The 2017 finding is an association [1], and the 2006 experiment compared a meat diet with a non-meat diet [3].

timeline.event: Havlicek and Lenochova report that non-meat diet body odor was rated more attractive than red-meat diet odor in Chemical Senses [3].
Zuniga et al. publish on diet quality and the attractiveness of male body odor [1].
